title: Whither quantum advantage? New classical lower bounds for Max-Cut on large-girth 3-regular graphs
authors: Flaviano Morone, Shivang Rawat, Dries Sels
abstract: Every 3-regular graph of girth at least $g$ has a cut containing at least a fraction $M_g$ of its edges, and the best rigorous bounds at large girth are $0.912\le \lim_{g\to\infty}M_g \le 0.92386$. Lower bounds on $M_g$ follow from the performance of local algorithms: on a graph of girth $g \ge 2p+2$ a depth-$p$ local algorithm sees the same tree around every edge, so its expected cut fraction on that tree bounds $M_g$ from below. We apply this strategy to the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL), a classical local algorithm, and evaluate it on the depth-$p$ tree for every even depth up to $p=32$. The resulting bounds exceed those recently obtained from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for every $p\ge 4$, by $0.005$ to $0.011$, and they extend the range of girths covered from $g=36$ to $g=66$. Notably, at $g=66$ we obtain $M_{66} \ge 0.9127$ at $99.99999\%$ confidence level, which raises the asymptotic lower bound from $0.912$ to $0.9127$.
summary: This work investigates the Max-Cut problem on large-girth 3-regular graphs to test for quantum advantage. By analyzing the local tree structure, the authors derive rigorous lower bounds using a classical local algorithm called VIRAL. These classical bounds surpass recent quantum bounds (QAOA) for several depths, suggesting that quantum advantage may not be guaranteed for this type of optimization problem.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the maximum cut fraction ($M_g$) for 3-regular graphs with large girth, specifically challenging the notion of quantum advantage in optimization.
main_result: A classical local algorithm (VIRAL) provides rigorous lower bounds on $M_g$ that exceed those from QAOA for even depths $p \ge 4$, suggesting a potential absence of quantum advantage for this specific problem.
method: The analysis leverages the fact that for large girth, the local structure around any edge is a tree, allowing the calculation of the expected cut fraction using local algorithms like VIRAL.
model_or_system: The model is the Max-Cut problem applied to 3-regular graphs whose girth $g$ is large. The analysis focuses on the local tree structure (radius-$p$ neighborhood) of these graphs.
key_observables: The maximum cut fraction $M_g = \inf_{G}  rac{	ext{MaxCut}(G)}{|E(G)|}$, and the expected cut fraction $c_{	ext{VIRAL}}(p)$ derived from local algorithms.
important_parameters: The girth $g$ (analyzed up to $g=66$) and the depth $p$ of the local algorithm ($p \le 32$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the graph girth $g \ge 2p+2$ to ensure the neighborhood structure is a tree, simplifying the calculation of the expected cut fraction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of the radius-2 neighborhood and plot the calculated cut fraction bounds for VIRAL, QAOA, and TPM across different depths $p$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical bounds for $M_g$, introduces the local algorithm (VIRAL), derives the lower bound based on the tree structure, and compares these classical bounds against established quantum bounds (QAOA).
why_interesting: The paper directly addresses the boundary of quantum advantage by showing that classical local algorithms can achieve bounds comparable to or exceeding those from QAOA for specific optimization problems on structured graphs.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Section of a 3-regular graph of girth g ≥6. The radius-2 neighborhood of an edge (u, v), consisting of the 14 vertices within distance 2 of u or v, and the 13 edges incident to u, v and their neighbors. The girth forces this tree structure. Any further edge among these vertices must join two leaves (since every other vertex already has degree 3) and it is allowed only if the two leaves lie on opposite sides of (u, v), where it closes a cycle of length 6 (dashed edge).

(3) these need the states at n = 1 of u, v and their four other neighbors a1, a2, b1, b2. No state of a leaf is needed at n = 1 or n = 2. (c), These six states need the seeds of all 14 vertices. The leaves enter only through their seeds, so the edges joining two leaves, such as the dashed one, play no role. Hence (σu, σv) is a fixed function of the 14 i.i.d. seeds on the tree of Fig. 1, the same for every edge of every 3-regular graph of girth g ≥6.
